newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich predicts House approval on disaster relief.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich predicts House approval on disaster relief.

text.p: The U.S. House of Representatives will move quickly next week to approve a disaster relief bill for the flood-ravaged Midwest, House Speaker Newt Gingrich said on Wednesday.
But the House Republican leadership will not strip the $8.4 billion emergency spending bill of unrelated spending and environmental amendments which President Clinton has threatened to veto.

The same measure threw Congress into chaos a week ago, when lawmakers tried to stop the House from adjourning for a week's break before a disaster aid measure could be approved. Members voted 67-278 to keep the chamber open, only to have the Republican leadership override their efforts by suspending business until June 3.

"I was disappointed it wasn't quite worked out. But I think we'll get it moved probably before the end of the first week when we're back, and I hope the president will sign it," Gingrich told reporters in his home district.

Congress and the White House have been unable to bridge their differences on the original disaster aid bill, which would provide $5.5 billion to more than 30 states hit by floods, mudslides and other natural disasters. The bill also included about $2 billion for U.S. overseas military operations.
The biggest hurdle has been a provision added by Republicans to keep the government open automatically next year if Congress and the White House failed to agree on needed spending bills.
Clinton threatened a veto over that plan, arguing that it would provide billions less for domestic spending than was allowed under a recent balanced-budget deal.

Asked if a stripped-down measure, like one offered unsuccessfully by House Appropriations Committee chairman Bob Livingston before the recess, would better serve the interests of people hit by disaster, Gingrich said Republicans would look instead to the national interest.

"It better serves the interests of the American people to keep the government open, and I think it better serves the interests of the American people to make sure that we're spending the money in a prudent manner," he said.

Gingrich, who left Washington before last Thursday's vote on adjournment, said Republican leaders decided to suspend House business because individual lawmakers had prior commitments, including some who joined the president on this week's NATO meeting.
But the speaker said House leaders postponed action on the bill only after learning that other federal assistance would be available to affected parts of the country.

"There's money in the pipeline. There's no danger of money running short. People can go ahead and continue to do the repair work. But I would like to see the bill get signed as early as possible," he said.
Lawmakers from flooded states have questioned whether enough money was available and have said the delay would only cause further uncertainty and expense.
